summary: An RCC runs search and rescue; 121.5 MHz is watched continuously, and the ATSU last in contact normally starts alerting action. For a SAR watch, file a flight plan, which is advisable more than 10 nm from the coast, over remote areas or without a suitable radio. Diverting? Tell the original destination before ETA plus 30 minutes or SAR action begins. The phases are uncertainty, alert and distress. If you see a craft in distress, keep it in sight, fix your position and report what you see. Ground signals: V assistance, X medical, arrow direction, Y yes, N no; the aircraft rocks its wings (day) or flashes its landing lights twice (night) to show it understood.
sections: Search and rescue in the UK
SAR is controlled by a Rescue Coordination Centre (RCC), acting on reports from any source; the response may be joint civil and military. Details: AIP GEN 3.6.
A continuous listening watch is kept on 121.5 MHz. If you can't make a Mayday, Pan or "lost" call on the frequency in use, call on 121.5.
Alerting service
Available to all aircraft known to ATS in the UK FIRs. Action is normally started by the ATSU last in contact with the aircraft, or the one that receives the information.
Position fixing on 121.5 MHz

The book describes autotriangulation (direction-finding fixes) on 121.5 MHz over much of England south and east of Manchester above 3,000 ft (down to 2,000 ft near London), triggered just by calling. The D&D cell can also use radar; check AIP GEN 3.6 for what's available now.
Transponder in an emergency
7700 emergency (keep an assigned code if already with a unit), 7600 radio failure, 7500 unlawful interference, with Mode C.
SAR watch
For a constant SAR watch, file a flight plan. Advisable when:
– flying more than 10 nm from the coast
– over remote or hazardous areas (northern Scotland, much of the west coast down to Cornwall)
– in an aircraft without a suitable radio
If you are expected at an aerodrome, tell its ATC unit (or the authority there) as soon as possible of:
– any change of destination
– any expected delay of 30 minutes or more
Diverting en route: tell the original destination (or ask ATC to) before your ETA plus 30 minutes, or SAR action will begin.
ICAO Annex 12
States provide SAR 24 hours a day in their territory, whatever the nationality of the aircraft or occupants.

Each State defines SAR regions (not overlapping) with a rescue coordination centre in each, coordinates with neighbouring States, and arranges for aircraft, ships and local services outside the SAR organisation to help.
Anyone who believes an aircraft is in an emergency passes all available information to the RCC immediately.
Emergency phases
Uncertainty phase: doubt about the safety of the aircraft. The RCC works with ATSUs to evaluate reports quickly.
Alert phase: concern for its safety. The RCC alerts SAR units and starts action.
Distress phase: reasonably certain the aircraft needs immediate assistance or faces grave and imminent danger. The RCC, in order:
– starts action by SAR units
– fixes the aircraft's position, its uncertainty and the search area
– notifies the operator, and adjacent RCCs if needed
– tells the ATSU about information from other sources
– asks aircraft, ships and coastal stations to listen for the aircraft or its ELT, help it and report
– makes and updates a SAR plan
– notifies the State of Registry and the accident investigation authorities
If you see an aircraft or vessel in distress (5.8)
Unless unable, or it's unnecessary:
– keep it in sight as long as needed
– fix your own position precisely

– report to the RCC or ATSU: type, identification and condition; its position (coordinates, or distance and true bearing from a landmark or navaid); time (UTC); number of people seen; whether they have abandoned it; number afloat; survivors' apparent condition
– act as instructed
The first aircraft on scene, if not a SAR aircraft, takes charge of on-scene activity until the first SAR aircraft arrives (or hands over to a capable aircraft if it can't talk to the RCC).
Directing a surface craft to the scene: give precise instructions by any means available.
If you intercept a distress call (5.9)
Record the aircraft's position if given; take a bearing if you can; inform the RCC or ATSU with all the information; at your discretion, head for the position while awaiting instructions.
Signals from survivors
Radio if it works, or: flares, a heliograph (mirror) flash, a flashing light, a flag (with a ball above or below it: the international distress signal), whistles, sea dye markers.
Ground-to-air signals, at least 2-3 m long, contrasting with the ground:
V: Require assistance
X: Require medical assistance
↑ (arrow): Proceeding in this direction
Y: Yes (affirmative)
N: No (negative)
Aircraft reply that the signal is understood: by day, rock the wings; at night, flash the landing lights on and off twice (or the navigation lights). No reply = not understood.
Memory aid V for "Very much need help", X marks a doctor's cross.

sum.Search and rescue in the UK: A Rescue Coordination Centre controls SAR; 121.5 MHz is watched continuously.
sum.Alerting service: For all aircraft known to ATS; the ATSU last in contact normally starts it.
sum.Position fixing on 121.5 MHz: Calling on 121.5 MHz lets the D&D cell fix your position.
sum.SAR watch: File a flight plan for a SAR watch; tell your destination of a diversion before ETA plus 30 minutes.
sum.ICAO Annex 12: SAR 24 hours a day for any nationality, in non-overlapping regions each with an RCC.
sum.Emergency phases: Uncertainty, then alert, then distress, each with more RCC action.
sum.If you see an aircraft or vessel in dist: Keep it in sight, fix your position, report what you see, follow instructions.
sum.If you intercept a distress call (5.9): Record the position, take a bearing, pass it on, and head there if appropriate.
sum.Signals from survivors: V assistance, X medical, arrow direction, Y yes, N no. Rock wings by day, flash lights twice at night.

cards.q: Who controls SAR in the UK?

cards.a: The ATSU last in contact with the aircraft.

cards.q: How do you get a SAR watch?
When is a flight plan advisable for SAR?
cards.a: More than 10 nm from the coast, over remote or hazardous areas, or without a suitable radio.

cards.q: Diverting en route: deadline to tell the original destination?
cards.a: Before ETA plus 30 minutes, or SAR action starts.
Reasonably certain the aircraft needs immediate help or faces grave and imminent danger.

cards.q: First non-SAR aircraft at a scene?
cards.a: Takes charge on scene until the first SAR aircraft arrives.

cards.q: Aircraft acknowledging a ground signal by day?

cards.a: Flashes its landing lights (or nav lights) on and off twice.

quiz.q: A survivor lays out a large 'X' on the ground. It means:
quiz.why: X is medical assistance; V is general assistance. The two are easy to swap.

quiz.q: A survivor lays out a 'V'. It means:
By day, a pilot shows that a ground signal has been understood by:
quiz.why: Rocking the wings by day; flashing the landing or navigation lights twice at night. No reply means not understood.

quiz.q: To get a constant SAR watch, a pilot should:
quiz.why: Filing a flight plan sets up the overdue action that triggers SAR.

quiz.q: A flight plan is advisable for SAR purposes when flying:
o: More than 10 nm from the coast, over remote areas, or without a suitable radio
More than 20 nm from the coast or over congested areas
Outside controlled airspace for more than an hour
More than 10 km from the coast
quiz.why: 10 nm (not km, not 20 nm), remote or hazardous areas, or no suitable radio.

quiz.q: You decide en route to land somewhere other than your flight-planned destination. You must tell the original destination:
o: Before your ETA there plus 30 minutes
Before your ETA there plus 60 minutes
Only if you were in controlled airspace
quiz.why: Otherwise overdue action and SAR start at ETA plus 30 minutes.

quiz.q: Which emergency phase is declared when there is concern for an aircraft's safety?
quiz.why: Uncertainty is doubt, alert is concern, distress is reasonable certainty of grave danger. 'Urgency' is a state of emergency, not a phase.

quiz.q: You see a boat sinking and you are the first aircraft on scene. You should:
o: Keep it in sight, fix your position and report to the RCC or ATSU
Leave the area so as not to hinder rescuers
Circle until you see the occupants rescued, without reporting
quiz.why: Keep sight, fix your own position, report type, position, time, numbers and condition, then act as instructed. You also take charge on scene until a SAR aircraft arrives.

quiz.q: An alerting service is provided by ATS to:
o: All aircraft known to ATS in the UK FIRs
Only aircraft on a flight plan
quiz.why: It is for all aircraft known to ATS; a flight plan just makes you known in advance.
